headline: JIT Compiling Code in 5μs is now easier with AI, enabling 20x speedups.
summary: A new approach, aided by AI, allows JIT compilers to achieve 5μs compilation times. This enables JIT compilation for every SQL query, not just a subset, significantly boosting performance.
details: Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, which generates code at runtime, can deliver significant performance gains, often 2-5x and sometimes over 20x. Historically, achieving fast JIT compilation was a complex task, requiring deep knowledge of assembly language.

Existing solutions like LLVM or C/C++ code generation suffer from high compile times, limiting their applicability in areas like databases. This meant many applications couldn't fully leverage the benefits of JIT.

However, with assistance from AI, writing fast JIT compilers by directly targeting assembly is now more accessible. This innovation allows for JIT compilation with extremely low overhead, making it feasible for broader use cases.

For instance, the pgrust project developed a JIT compiler that compiles code in approximately 5 microseconds (5μs). This speed allows pgrust to JIT compile every SQL query, rather than being limited to a subset.

The process involves two main steps: generating the assembly code and then packaging it into a callable function. A key technique used is 'copy-and-patch,' which utilizes assembly 'stencils' that are tweaked for specific operations.

This method allows for constructing runtime programs with performance comparable to handwritten code. Benchmarks show a JIT-compiled regular expression engine performing nearly 20x faster than an interpreter, matching handwritten performance.

headline_marked: [[Wi-Fi 8 focuses on reliability]], not speed, targeting 25% better throughput and lower latency
headline: Wi-Fi 8 focuses on reliability, not speed, targeting 25% better throughput and lower latency
summary: Wi-Fi 8, dubbed "Ultra High Reliability" by IEEE, aims to significantly improve network stability, effective throughput, and reduce latency by 25% in real-world scenarios.
details: Wi-Fi 8, officially dubbed "Ultra High Reliability" by IEEE, marks a significant shift from previous generations by prioritizing reliability over raw speed. While Wi-Fi 7 already offers 23 Gbit/s per band, Wi-Fi 8 will maintain similar maximum data rates, spatial streams, and modulation.

Instead, the new standard focuses on improving effective throughput and reducing latency by 25% in 95th percentile scenarios. It also aims to decrease MAC protocol data unit loss by 25% and increase throughput at various signal-to-interference-and-noise ratio (SINR) levels by 25%.

Key features include Distributed-tone resource units (DRUs), which allow devices to spread transmissions across wider bandwidth for more reliable connectivity, especially useful for low-power smart home devices. Interference mitigation pilots will help resist unexpected interference in unlicensed bands.

Wi-Fi 8 will also leverage unequal modulations, adjusting each spatial stream's modulation individually based on SINR for greater efficiency. New Modulation and Coding Schemes (MCS) are being added to further improve throughput.

Latency reductions are achieved through features like P-EDCA, which speeds up channel access for prioritized devices. The standard also allows communication on non-primary channels even when the primary is busy, reducing wasted bandwidth.
Other improvements target seamless roaming between access points, aiming for near-zero downtime. It will also enhance connectivity when using multiple access points simultaneously.

Expected to be finalized in 2028, Wi-Fi 8 is positioned to compete with 6G cellular networks in handling massive numbers of connected devices. This focus on real-world performance in crowded environments is a major departure from speed-centric upgrades.
